The author is Omri Ben-Shahar, and the subtitle is [How Privacy Panic Led Tech Regulation Astray -- and How to Fix It](https://marginalrevolution.com?action=user_content_redirect&uuid=b3161e81822d2af970dda4967fc8adc1539336cf12788c79eba1b12d74b17e8a&blog_id=42693868&post_id=93864&user_id=262258391&subs_id=225460721&signature=984ad4f99b115c475cc49ee6c6fade71&email_name=new-post&user_email=ishan.mail@gmail.com&encoded_&email_id=c06311760f5d9560969a838c316634a0). I would describe this book as bracing, and full of substantive engagement. Basically the author wishes to give privacy considerations less weight in social decisions. Excerpt:
What is the concrete evidence for the benefits of facial recognition technology in investigation of human-trafficking crimes? I would love to have found global estimates of the magnitude -- of the trafficking victims rescued through the most advanced facial recognition methods -- but all I have is a collage of reports [reports are then described].
One chapter is entitled "The Futility of Personal Rights." Agree or not, this book is full of actual arguments, so I approve.
